chapters.title: Chapter 5: Reconciling Everything Before You File

lessons.title: Pre-filled ITR Data, Mismatches and the Notices They Trigger

children.text: Open the return form on the e-filing portal and much of it is already filled in: your salary, your interest, your dividends, your TDS. It is tempting to click through and submit. That convenience is also a trap. The pre-filled data is only as good as the information behind it, and it cannot see what nobody reported. After you file, the same information is used to check your return, and every gap becomes a message, an adjustment or a notice.

body.text: The pre-filled return is the department's first guess about your income. Treat it as a draft to correct, not an answer to accept.

children.text: Where the Pre-filled Data Comes From

body.caption: What pre-fills, and what you still need to check

cells: Personal details and bank account
Your e-filing profile
Address, and a pre-validated bank account for any refund
Salary
Salary information reported by employers
Gross salary per employer, and that a previous employer's salary is not counted twice
Interest and dividends
Derived values in TIS
Every account is included, duplicates removed, joint income correctly attributed
Capital gains, in forms that have that schedule
Securities and mutual fund data in TIS
Sale values, cost and holding periods, against your broker's tax P&L
TDS and TCS
Form 26AS
Every credit is present and none belongs to someone else
Advance and self-assessment tax
Challan data, shown in AIS
Every challan you paid appears

body.text: Pre-fill cannot see what was never reported: rent received without TDS, freelance income paid by individuals, foreign income, or gains on crypto bought on a foreign exchange. It also does not know your exemptions and deductions under the old regime unless you enter them. Your reconciliation from the last lesson, not the pre-fill, decides what goes in your return.

children.text: Returns are processed centrally and largely automatically. The system compares what you reported with Form 26AS, Form 16 and AIS. What happens next depends on the size and type of the mismatch, and on when it is found.

cells: Nudge
Email or SMS from the department
AIS shows transactions that your return seems not to reflect
Review AIS and file a revised or updated return if you did miss something
Proposed adjustment
Communication under section 143(1)(a) of the 1961 Act, before processing
Income in Form 26AS or Form 16 not included in your return, or a claim that looks incorrect
Agree or disagree online within 30 days, with reasons
Intimation
Intimation after processing, showing tax payable or refund
Processing completed, with or without adjustments
If an adjustment is wrong, seek rectification
e-Verification
Notice on the compliance portal asking for an explanation
AIS information that appears unreported or under-reported in your return
Explain with evidence on the compliance portal, or correct your return
Scrutiny or reassessment
Formal notice for detailed examination
Larger or unexplained mismatches, or income that has escaped assessment
Respond with full documentation, usually with professional help

body.text: Processing moves to section 270 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (section 143(1) of the 1961 Act) for returns from tax year 2026-27. The logic is the same: specified adjustments can be made only after telling you and considering your response, and the intimation must be sent within nine months from the end of the financial year in which the return is filed.

children.text: The most common mismatch notice for salaried taxpayers is a proposed adjustment. One adjustment the law specifically allows is adding income that appears in Form 26AS or Form 16 but is missing from your return. Before making it, the department must tell you and invite a response. If you do not respond within 30 days, the return is processed with the adjustment.

You can agree, if you really did miss the income, or disagree, if the data is wrong or you reported the income elsewhere. Disagreeing is not risky when you have a genuine reason. Silence is what costs money.

Nikhil, a data engineer in Bengaluru, switched jobs in October 2025. His first employer paid ₹6,00,000 and his second paid ₹9,00,000. He had submitted Form 12B, so his second employer's Form 16 showed the earlier ₹6,00,000 in row 1(e). He correctly reported total salary of ₹15,00,000.
In September 2026 he receives a proposed adjustment adding ₹6,00,000 of salary, because the system read the old salary from both certificates.

body.caption: What the proposed adjustment assumed, and what was true

cells: Salary from first employer
Salary from second employer
Previous salary in second employer's row 1(e)
₹6,00,000 added again
Already counted above
Total salary

children.text: Nikhil logs in, chooses to disagree, and explains that row 1(e) of his second Form 16 repeats salary already reported from his first employer, attaching both Form 16s. Had he ignored it, ₹6,00,000 would have been added to his income.
Fixing Your Own Mistakes Before They Ask
If you find a mistake yourself, the cheapest time to fix it is now. You have two tools.

columns.label: Revised return
points: Section 139(5) of the 1961 Act for FY 2025-26
Fixes any mistake or omission, in either direction
Can increase a refund or reduce tax
For FY 2025-26, file by 31 December 2026 to avoid any fee
No additional tax beyond the tax and interest actually due

columns.label: Updated return (ITR-U)
points: Section 263(6)(a) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (section 139(8A) of the 1961 Act)
Only to report more income or pay more tax
Cannot be used to increase a refund or reduce tax
Available up to 48 months from the end of the assessment year
Comes with additional tax that rises the longer you wait

body.title: Additional tax on an updated return
body.xAxisLabel: Filed within this many months from the end of the assessment year
body.yAxisLabel: Additional tax as % of tax and interest due

body.caption: Rate is 25%, 50%, 60% or 70% depending on when the updated return is filed

body.title: The 30-day window
body.question: Seema receives a proposed adjustment adding ₹48,000 of interest that appears in her Form 26AS. She is travelling and does not respond. What happens after 30 days?
options: Nothing, because adjustments need her consent
Her return is processed with the ₹48,000 added
Her return is automatically sent for scrutiny
The adjustment lapses and she gets a refund
body.explanation: If no response is received within 30 days of the intimation, the return is processed incorporating the adjustment. She would then have to seek rectification if the adjustment was wrong.

body.title: Cost of waiting
body.prompt: Imran missed some income in his FY 2025-26 return. When he files an updated return, the tax due on the missed income plus interest comes to ₹14,000. If he files within 24 months from the end of the assessment year, how much additional tax does he pay on top of the ₹14,000?
body.explanation: Within 24 months the rate is 50%: 50% × ₹14,000 = ₹7,000, making ₹21,000 in total. Within 12 months it would have been 25%, or ₹3,500. Fixing it in a revised return before 31 December 2026 would have cost only the tax and interest.

body.title: Where to answer e-verification
body.textWithBlank: Responses to e-verification notices about AIS mismatches are submitted on the income tax ___ portal, not by email.
body.explanation: e-Verification notices and responses are handled on the compliance portal, reached through the e-filing portal.

body.title: Divya's nudge email
body.scenario: Divya, an architect employed by a firm in Jaipur, filed her FY 2025-26 return in July 2026 using the pre-filled data. In October 2026 she gets an email from the department saying AIS shows transactions not reflected in her return. Checking AIS, she finds ₹18,000 of dividends from shares held with her husband's demat account, which she forgot, and a ₹5,00,000 SFT-010 mutual fund purchase.
body.prompt: What should Divya do, and how urgently?
body.modelAnswer: She should act quickly while the cheapest fix is available. First, check whether the shares are held in her name: if the dividends are hers, she should report them. The SFT-010 purchase is not income, so it needs no change to the return, though she should be able to explain the source of funds. Since it is before 31 December 2026, she can file a revised return for FY 2025-26 including the ₹18,000 of dividends and paying any extra tax and interest, with no additional tax. If she waits past the revised return window, she would need an updated return with 25% or more additional tax, and an unanswered mismatch could lead to an e-verification notice.

body.title: Reviewing your pre-filled return
steps: Compare every pre-filled salary figure with each Form 16, watching for salary counted twice after a job switch.
Check interest and dividends against your reconciliation worksheet, not just TIS.
Replace sale values with actual capital gains from your broker and fund statements.
Confirm every TDS and TCS entry against Form 26AS, and every challan against AIS.
Add income nobody reported, such as rent without TDS or foreign income.
Enter exemptions and deductions you are eligible for, with proof ready.
After filing, watch your email and the e-filing portal, and respond to any proposed adjustment within 30 days.

points: Pre-filled data comes from TIS, Form 26AS and your profile. It is a draft, not a finished return.
Pre-fill misses income nobody reported and does not know your old-regime exemptions and deductions.
Mismatches escalate from nudges to proposed adjustments, intimations, e-verification and scrutiny.
A proposed adjustment gives you 30 days to agree or disagree. No response means the adjustment is made.
Fix your own mistakes early with a revised return. An updated return costs 25% to 70% extra.
From tax year 2026-27, processing is under section 270 and updated returns under section 263(6)(a) of the Income-tax Act, 2025.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and reflects rules as of September 2026. Deadlines and fees for revised returns may change through Budget amendments. Names and amounts are illustrative. For any notice you receive, read it carefully and consider consulting a chartered accountant.
